clue.text: Tricky phrase that might produce stuttering woe?

indicators.note: the answer, twisted about, would produce the clue's last two words, so they are the letters to rearrange

blocks.note: the fodder, both words letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone trips over a hard sentence and ends up stammering miserably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuttering woe' reads as the effect of saying the phrase; it is the thirteen letters to rearrange, and 'twister' in the answer hints at the twisting.
explanation.definitionFit: A deliberately awkward sequence of sounds, recited as a game, that trips the speaker's mouth into errors.

clue.text: One that might be brewing or poaching?

blocks.note: the leaves steep in the pot while a cuppa brews
Cockney rhyming slang for a thief, and a poacher steals game

explanation.surface: Something in the kitchen might be brewing or poaching, like a cook's two methods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brewing or poaching' looks like two cooking verbs; the second really points to theft. TEA LEAF is Cockney rhyming slang for thief, and a poacher steals game.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang turns thief into this phrase, so one stealing game qualifies; literally it also steeps in hot water.

clue.text: Makes dull songs without hesitation

indicators.note: 'without' means lacking, so the songs word must lose the hesitation sound

blocks.note: musical pieces in a show or set are called numbers
the sound a speaker makes while hesitating

explanation.surface: A critic complains that some tediously sung tracks deaden the listener, delivered without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Songs' is the fodder word, not a subject: in a show or concert each song is a number.
explanation.definitionFit: To deaden feeling or sensation in someone is a straightforward synonym for this verb.

clue.text: Pursued, trounced, commandeered

indicators.note: something trounced is thrashed and knocked about, so the letters of 'Pursued' get battered into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Three past-tense verbs from a battle report: chased, beaten, then seized.
explanation.walkthrough: With three verbs in a row any could be the definition; only the last matches the enumeration once the first is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking something, such as a throne or power, by force without right is a close synonym.

clue.text: Primarily, trendy educational disquisition to advance latest knowledge?

definitions.text: Primarily, trendy educational disquisition to advance latest knowledge?

indicators.note: 'primarily' means first of all, so take the opening letter of each following word

blocks.clueFragment: trendy educational disquisition to advance latest knowledge
blocks.note: initial letters of the seven words that follow

explanation.surface: A description of a fashionable lecture meant to push the frontier of knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: its initials spell the answer, and it describes one fairly.
explanation.definitionFit: Short, fashionable filmed lectures from the TED conferences spread new ideas to wide online audiences.

clue.text: Sort of raid, no?

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant version, so the letters of 'raid, no' come in a different order

blocks.note: the fodder, both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A doubtful question: was it a kind of raid, or not?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: shuffle RAID NO for the letters, and read it as a description, since an inroad is a sort of raid.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostile incursion into enemy territory is the original military sense, close kin to a foray.

clue.text: Even now, toady's hit ferociously

indicators.note: done ferociously, the words 'toady's hit' are savaged and their letters torn into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A sycophant is still getting hit hard, even at this late stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toady' looks like a person to define; it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean still, up to the present moment, as in 'she remembers it still'.

clue.text: Malodorous, the French starter of snails causes vexation

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so only the opening letter of 'snails' is used

blocks.note: rank means foul-smelling
the French masculine 'the'
opening letter of snails

explanation.surface: A diner is annoyed by a smelly French starter of snails, escargots gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French starter of snails' reads as escargots on a menu; 'the French' is LE and 'starter' is just the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: When a grievance goes on irritating someone, it is said to keep annoying or festering in them.

clue.text: Some herbal medicine?

indicators.note: 'some' asks for only a part, so the answer is a run of letters inside 'herbal medicine'

blocks.note: the run spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Asking for a portion of a plant-based remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the letters sit inside herBAL Medicine, and a balm is indeed a herbal remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A soothing ointment, often plant-derived, used on skin or wounds; lemon balm is also a herb.

clue.text: Get below platform

blocks.note: a plain synonym
a raised stage or stall

explanation.surface: An instruction to climb down under a stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' reads as a command to move; it is the definition, in the sense 'I get it'.
explanation.definitionFit: In casual speech to grasp or follow an idea, as in 'I get it', is this verb.

clue.text: Extremely fertile cat returned to admit misdeeds

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so keep only the outer letters of 'fertile'
something returned goes back the way it came, so the word for 'cat' runs backwards

blocks.note: first and last letters of fertile
an informal word for a cat

explanation.surface: A very fertile cat is brought back so someone can own up to wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like it intensifies 'fertile'; it means take the extremes, F and E.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal phrasal verb for confessing, owning up to something done wrong.

clue.text: Burrowing creature loses daughter, runs forward to reach Texan city

indicators.note: the burrowing animal's name loses the letter standing for 'daughter'
the 'runs' letter moves forward along the word, a local rearrangement of what is left

blocks.note: the armoured American mammal that digs burrows
the standard abbreviation in family trees

explanation.surface: An armadillo, having lost its young, hurries on to a Texas town.
explanation.walkthrough: Take D out of ARMADILLO to get ARMAILLO, then shift R (runs, as in cricket scoring) two places later in the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in the Texas Panhandle, known from the song about getting to it by morning.

clue.text: Piece of British landscape depicted in off-key, sad composition

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters of 'off-key, sad' are arranged afresh

blocks.note: the fodder, hyphen and comma ignored

explanation.surface: A melancholy, out-of-tune piece of music paints a British scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composition' looks musical, fitting 'off-key'; it is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An eighth-century earthwork bank built by King Offa of Mercia, running along the England-Wales border.

clue.text: McEwan novel, Decapitated Pet Cuckoo’s Upset

indicators.note: to decapitate is to cut off the head, so the pet loses its first letter
in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word for 'cuckoo' reads upwards

blocks.note: a small rodent kept as a pet
cuckoo means crazy

explanation.surface: Styled as a book title: a headless pet cuckoo is distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics dress the wordplay as a title. HAMSTER minus H leaves AMSTER; MAD reversed is DAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan's 1998 Booker Prize winner is named after the Dutch capital where it ends.

clue.text: Puts on about 500 commercials

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the commercials word goes around the numeral

blocks.note: short for advertisements
D is the Roman numeral 500

explanation.surface: A broadcaster schedules about five hundred advertisements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About 500' reads as an approximate count; 'about' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To put on something, like weight or extra charges, is to increase it by that amount.

clue.text: Very good ... very good ... distinctly average

blocks.note: 'very' is so, as in 'so good'
the same trick a second time

explanation.surface: A lukewarm review: 'very good... very good...' trailing off into plain mediocre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very good' is not praise here: 'very' is SO, and 'good' just keeps the phrase natural. Twice over gives SO-SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Neither good nor bad, merely middling or mediocre, is what this reduplicated expression describes.

clue.text: Sit around, loiter endlessly with contemptuous expression

indicators.note: 'Sit' goes around, so its letters surround the shortened loitering word
without an end, the word for 'loiter' loses its last letter

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
to hang about in one place

explanation.surface: Someone lounges and idles, sneering at anyone who objects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sit' is used as it stands, as letters, not as an action; the loitering word sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rude, dismissive retort telling someone you reject what they offer or say.

clue.text: Unpleasant haircut that might be seen at tea time

definitions.text: that might be seen at tea time
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: something seen at tea time

blocks.note: a sticky situation is an awkward, nasty one
hair gathered into a knot at the back of the head

explanation.surface: An ugly hairstyle spotted at afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: A bun is strictly a hairstyle rather than a cut, but the setter stretches it; the definition is a descriptive phrase for the cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet glazed bread roll, often with icing or syrup, typically served with a cup of tea in Britain.

clue.text: Little bird going round city in direction of very little one

indicators.note: the bird goes round, so its letters encircle the city and direction words

blocks.note: a small songbird, as in blue tit
abbreviation for New York
as in 'heading to town'

explanation.surface: A small bird circles a city, flying towards a tiny chick.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the city and the direction word go inside the bird together; NY for New York is a standard crossword city.
explanation.definitionFit: An affectionate phrase for a small child, a toddler, doubling up on smallness.

clue.text: Instigator of Brexit vote: ‘Country will lose nothing’

indicators.note: the country's name will lose the letter that looks like zero

blocks.note: the Central African nation
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A campaign slogan warning that the nation will lose out entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one O from CAMEROON. The quote reads like a Brexit prophecy.
explanation.definitionFit: David Cameron, UK Prime Minister, called the 2016 referendum on leaving the European Union.

clue.text: A little unwisely, skull cap removed for heavy metal

indicators.note: a little of the word means just its opening letter
removing the cap takes off the top, so the skull word loses its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of unwisely
the bony case of the head

explanation.surface: Someone rashly takes off a skull cap to headbang to heavy metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy metal' suggests music; here it is literal, a dense chemical element. CRANIUM minus C gives RANIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A dense radioactive element with a very high atomic weight, fuel for nuclear reactors.

clue.text: Lunatic overcome by boundless ocean, misrepresented?

definitions.text: Lunatic overcome by boundless ocean, misrepresented?

indicators.note: without bounds the word 'ocean' loses both its ends
misrepresented means shown wrongly, so the remaining ocean letters are jumbled
overcome by means swamped, so the lunatic is engulfed by the ocean letters

blocks.note: ocean without first and last letters
slang for a crazy person

explanation.surface: A madman swamped by the sea, whose story has been told wrongly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: King Canute is wrongly remembered as a fool who ordered the tide back, when he did it to show the limits of royal power.
explanation.definitionFit: The eleventh-century king of England, Denmark and Norway, famous for the legend of commanding the waves.

clue.text: Alert: ‘Following boundary, Australian captain declared’

indicators.note: something declared is said out loud, so both cricket words are taken by their sound
the captain comes following the boundary, so his piece is placed second

blocks.note: in cricket a ball reaching the rope along the ground scores four
Shane Warne, the leg-spinner, who captained Australia in one-day games

explanation.surface: A cricket news flash: the Australian skipper declared after hitting a boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declared' is a cricket term for ending an innings; here it signals sound. A boundary is a four; Shane Warne was a famous Australian cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone advance notice of danger, putting them on guard beforehand.

clue.text: Duchess, low in rank, obtaining grand husband?

indicators.note: to obtain something is to take it in, so the word for low status holds the other two

blocks.note: mean can mean humble, of low birth
slang for a thousand pounds, abbreviated
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A duchess of humble rank married a grand husband, a nod to a royal wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: G and H go inside MEAN. The question mark nods to Meghan's marriage to Prince Harry.
explanation.definitionFit: Meghan Markle became Duchess of Sussex on marrying Prince Harry in 2018.

clue.text: Perhaps Guitar Hero fan offering a bit of Young Americans

indicators.note: only a bit of 'Young Americans' is wanted, a run of consecutive letters inside

blocks.note: the run spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A music video-game fan plays a snatch of the David Bowie album.
explanation.walkthrough: Both italic titles look like music: Guitar Hero is a video game, and Young Americans is a Bowie album hiding younG AMERicans.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who plays video games; Guitar Hero is one example, hence 'Perhaps'.

clue.text: ‘Executive Search’ pro haunted her disturbingly

indicators.note: things disturbed are thrown out of order, so the letters of 'haunted her' get rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: A recruitment professional has creepily haunted a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Executive search is the formal name for recruiting senior staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A recruiter who approaches senior staff to lure them into new jobs at other firms.

clue.text: Extensive head of hair, we’re told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so go by the sound of the hair word

blocks.note: a mane is a long, thick head of hair

explanation.surface: Someone is said to have a huge, bushy head of hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extensive' seems to describe the hair; it is the definition, in the old sense of main as vast, as in 'the main' for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense of the word meant great in size or force, as in 'with might and main'.

clue.text: Team Trump rent asunder, leading to explosion of rage

indicators.note: torn asunder means ripped apart, so the letters of 'Team Trump rent' are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: the fodder, all three words
